summary: Defines the UPDATE method for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP). It lets a client change session parameters, such as media streams and codecs, without affecting the dialog state. Unlike a re-INVITE, it can be sent before the initial INVITE has finished, which suits early dialogs.

plainLanguage.summary: SIP normally uses one message, INVITE, both to set up a call and to change it later. That message also changes the state of the call itself, which stops it being used for some changes. RFC 3311 adds UPDATE, a lighter request that changes only the media settings and can even be sent before the call is answered.

subtitle: A SIP request that changes a session's media settings without touching the dialog, even before the call is answered.

tldr.problem: A SIP re-INVITE changes both the session and the dialog state, so it cannot be used to change media settings such as putting early media on hold before the initial INVITE has been answered.
tldr.mechanism: The UPDATE method carries an SDP offer inside an existing dialog, early or confirmed, and the answer comes back in the 2xx response to the UPDATE. It has no effect on the dialog state.
tldr.outcome: Either side can adjust session parameters while the call is still ringing. On confirmed dialogs the RFC still recommends a re-INVITE, because UPDATE must be answered immediately and so leaves no room for the user to approve.

facts.label: Retry delay after 491
facts.value: 2.1 to 4 s if it owns the Call-ID, otherwise 0 to 2 s

today: RFC 3311 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2002, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It remains the definition of the SIP UPDATE method.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SIP defines the INVITE method for the initiation and modification of sessions. That method affects two important pieces of state: the session, meaning the media streams SIP sets up, and the dialog, meaning the state that SIP itself defines. Coupling the two is reasonable in many cases but causes complications in others.

The primary difficulty arises when aspects of the session need to be modified before the initial INVITE has been answered. One example is early media, where the session is established to convey progress of the call but the INVITE itself is not yet accepted. It matters that either the caller or the callee be able to modify the characteristics of that session, for example putting the early media on hold, before the call is answered. A re-INVITE cannot be used for this, because it has an impact on the state of the dialog as well as on the session.

UPDATE fulfills that need. It can be sent by a user agent within a dialog, early or confirmed, to update session parameters without impacting the dialog state itself.
sections.plainLanguage: A SIP INVITE does two jobs at once: it sets up the call and it changes the call. UPDATE is a separate, lighter message that only does the second job, so a call can be adjusted without disturbing the state of the conversation.

sections.title: Overview of Operation
sections.content:
Operation of this extension is straightforward. The caller begins with an INVITE transaction, which proceeds normally. Once a dialog is established, whether early or confirmed, the caller can generate an UPDATE that contains an SDP offer for the purpose of updating the session. The response to the UPDATE contains the answer.

Similarly, once a dialog is established, the callee can send an UPDATE with an offer, and the caller places its answer in the 2xx response to the UPDATE. The Allow header field is used to indicate support for the UPDATE method. There are additional constraints on when UPDATE can be used, based on the restrictions of the offer and answer model.
sections.plainLanguage: Either side of a call can send an UPDATE carrying a new description of the media, and the other side answers in the reply. The two sides take turns doing this while the call is still being set up.

sections.title: Determining Support for the Extension
sections.content:
The initiation of a session operates as specified in RFC 3261. However, a user agent compliant with this specification SHOULD also include an Allow header field in the INVITE request, listing the method UPDATE, to indicate its ability to receive an UPDATE request.

When a user agent server compliant with this specification receives an INVITE request for a new dialog and generates a reliable provisional response containing SDP, that response SHOULD contain an Allow header field listing the UPDATE method. This informs the caller that the callee is capable of receiving an UPDATE request at any time. An unreliable provisional response MAY contain such an Allow header field, and a 2xx response SHOULD contain one as well.

Responses are processed normally as per RFC 3261, and in the case of reliable provisional responses according to RFC 3262. A reliable provisional response always creates an early dialog at the user agent client, and creation of that dialog is necessary in order to receive UPDATE requests from the callee. If the response contains an Allow header field with the value UPDATE, the client knows the callee supports UPDATE and may follow the sending procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: Before using UPDATE, a caller checks whether the other end supports it. The callee says so by listing UPDATE in the Allow header of its reply to the first INVITE.

sections.title: Sending an UPDATE
sections.content:
The UPDATE request is constructed as would any other request within an existing dialog. It MAY be sent for both early and confirmed dialogs, and MAY be sent by either the caller or the callee. Although UPDATE can be used on confirmed dialogs, it is RECOMMENDED that a re-INVITE be used instead. The reason is that an UPDATE needs to be answered immediately, which rules out the possibility of user approval. Such approval will frequently be needed, and it is possible with a re-INVITE.

UPDATE is a target refresh request, so it can update the remote target of a dialog. If a user agent uses an UPDATE request or response to modify the remote target while an INVITE transaction is in progress, and it is the user agent server for that INVITE transaction, it MUST place the same value into the Contact header field of the 2xx to the INVITE as it placed into the UPDATE.

The rules for inclusion of offers and answers in SIP messages still apply, because they exist to guarantee a consistent view of the session state. These rules set out, for the caller and for the callee, when an UPDATE may carry an offer. In short, an UPDATE may carry an offer only when every other offer already in flight has been answered, and when any offer the sender received has been answered.
sections.plainLanguage: An UPDATE may carry a new media offer only when the two sides are not juggling several offers at once. Any offer already sent must have been answered first, so both ends always agree on what the session is.

sections.title: Receiving an UPDATE and Its Response
sections.content:
The UPDATE is processed as any other mid-dialog target refresh request. If the request is generally acceptable, processing continues as described below. A user agent server that receives an UPDATE before it has generated a final response to a previous UPDATE on the same dialog MUST return a 500 response to the new UPDATE and MUST include a Retry-After header field with a randomly chosen value between 0 and 10 seconds.

If an UPDATE is received that contains an offer, and the server has generated an offer to which it has not yet received an answer, it MUST reject the UPDATE with a 491 response. If the server has received an offer to which it has not yet generated an answer, it MUST reject the UPDATE with a 500 response and include a Retry-After header field with a value between 0 and 10 seconds.

On receiving an UPDATE for an existing dialog, the user agent MUST check the version identifiers in the session description, or the content of the session description if there are none, to see whether it has changed. If it has changed, the server MUST adjust the session parameters and generate an answer in the 2xx response. However, unlike a re-INVITE, the UPDATE MUST be responded to promptly, so the user cannot generally be prompted to approve the changes. If the server cannot change the session parameters without prompting the user, it SHOULD reject the request with a 504 response. If the new session description is not acceptable, the server can reject it with a 488 response, and that response SHOULD include a Warning header field.

At the client, a non-2xx final response to an UPDATE means the session parameters MUST remain unchanged, as if no UPDATE had been issued. A 481 response, a 408 response, or no response at all causes the client to terminate the dialog. If the client receives a 491 response, it SHOULD start a timer whose value is randomly chosen between 2.1 and 4 seconds in units of 10 ms when it owns the Call-ID of the dialog, and between 0 and 2 seconds otherwise. When the timer fires, the client SHOULD attempt the UPDATE once more if it still wants the session modification to happen.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiving side either accepts the new settings and answers with its own, or turns the request down with a status code that says why. If both sides happen to change the call at the same moment, the loser retries after a short random delay.

sections.title: Example Call Flow
sections.content:
The RFC presents an example call flow using the UPDATE method. The caller sends an initial INVITE with an offer. The callee generates a 180 response with an answer to that offer. With the completion of the offer and answer exchange the session is established, although the dialog is still in the early state.

The caller generates a PRACK to acknowledge the 180, and the PRACK is answered with a 200 OK. The caller then decides to update some aspect of the session, to put it on hold for example, and generates an UPDATE request with a new offer. That offer is answered in the 200 response to the UPDATE. Shortly afterward the callee decides to update some aspect of the session in turn, so it generates an UPDATE request with an offer, and the answer is sent in the 200 response. Finally the callee answers the call, resulting in a 200 OK response to the INVITE and then an ACK. Neither the 200 OK to the INVITE nor the ACK will contain SDP.
sections.plainLanguage: The example shows a call being set up while both sides change the media settings twice, once each, and then finally being answered. The call settings can be changed while the phone is still ringing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations for UPDATE are identical to those for re-INVITE. It is important that the UPDATE be integrity protected and authenticated as coming from the same source as the entity on the other end of the dialog. RFC 3261 discusses the security mechanisms for achieving these functions.
sections.plainLanguage: An UPDATE must be protected and checked in the same way as the original INVITE, so that only the party on the other end of the call can ask for a change.

items.label: SERVER BUSY
items.desc: An earlier UPDATE on the same dialog has not been answered yet. A Retry-After header with a value of 0 to 10 seconds must be included.

items.label: REQUEST TERMINATED
items.desc: The receiver has sent an offer that has not been answered yet, so the incoming offer must be rejected.

items.label: SERVER TIME-OUT
items.desc: The receiver cannot change the session without asking the user, and UPDATE has to be answered immediately.

items.label: NOT ACCEPTABLE HERE
items.desc: The new session description is not acceptable. The response should carry a Warning header field.

items.label: CALL DOES NOT EXIST
items.desc: At the client, this ends the dialog.
